items.heard_summary: The first audio window (22.6–27.7s) consists entirely of percussion and a rhythmic ostinato without a clear pitched melody. In the second window (starting at 31.0s), a distinct melodic line enters, played by a wind-like or synthesized lead instrument. The melody prominently features the intervallic sequence A – B♭ – C♯, moving by a semitone and then an augmented second (three semitones).
specific_findings: Clip 1 confirms the presence of only drums and an ostinato before the melody enters.
Clip 2 verifies the emergence of the pitched melody at approximately 31 seconds.
The audible succession of A, B♭, and C♯ (1, ♭2, ♯3) creates the characteristic augmented second of the Hijaz/Arabic mode, directly supporting the submitted explanation and Choice D.

The alternative analysis is sound: Phrygian (1, ♭2, ♭3) is ruled out because the melody clearly ascends to a raised third (C♯) rather than a minor third (C natural), and the augmented second is too prominent to be ignored.
items.uncertainty: No significant uncertainty; the augmented second interval is acoustically distinct and firmly establishes the Arabic/Hijaz modal flavor over the other options.

items.heard_summary: In the first supplied window, the harmony moves from a preparatory sonority near the beginning of the excerpt to a dominant-colored E–G♯–B collection and then to an A–C–E collection, giving a clear dominant-to-A-minor resolution. The second window contains a comparable preparation–tension–resolution gesture. The overall effect is best described as a ii–V–i-type motion in A minor, heard as the vi area of C, rather than a progression that stops on a C-major dominant.
specific_findings: Near original 6.4 s, the audible pitch content includes E, G♯, and B, producing dominant pull toward A.
Near original 8.4 s, the following sonority includes A, C, and E, confirming resolution to A minor rather than return to C major.
A preceding preparatory chord is present around original 4 s, consistent with the ii part of a ii–V–i in A minor, though the submitted explanation does not specify its exact pitches or voicing.
The later window, original 15.85–25.29 s, repeats a similar preparation–dominant–resolution pattern, supporting the claimed harmonic behavior.
The alternative I–ii–V reading is not supported because the excerpt does not treat the dominant as the final goal; it resolves to the A-minor/vi area.
items.uncertainty: No score region was supplied, so score-region relevance is not applicable. The exact quality/voicing of the preparatory ii chord and the broader C-major context before the first window are not fully specified in the submitted evidence; the supported core is the audible E-major dominant to A-minor resolution and the repeated tension–release pattern.

items.heard_summary: The exposed ukulele intro presents the pitch collection A–C–E–G, with A recurring and C, E, and G sounding around it. No B-flat or E-flat is audible. The sonority matches a C6/Am7 open-string collection, and the overall emphasis is more consistent with a C-major six-chord reading than with a plain A-minor triad, A diminished, or C7.
specific_findings: Audible notes include A, C, E, and G, which correspond to C–E–G–A, the submitted C6 explanation.
A plain A minor triad would be A–C–E and does not account for the audible G.
A diminished would require E-flat, which is not present.
C7 would require B-flat, which is not present.
The alternative analysis correctly notes that Am7 and C6 share the same pitch collection, so the final label depends on harmonic center/context.
No score region was supplied, so score-region relevance is not applicable.
items.uncertainty: The pitch collection is clear, but the root/harmonic center is somewhat interpretive because Am7 and C6 contain the same notes. I did not verify an isolated bass pedal or definitive root beyond the audible contextual emphasis toward C.

items.heard_summary: The closing excerpt is decisively a dominant-to-tonic ending: a G-based dominant sonority with tension resolves to a C-major tonic, which is then sustained/decays to the end. An earlier minor-colored preparation is present but less sharply separable than the final V–I motion. The ending does not sound like F-to-C plagal, does not stop on V, and does not deceive to vi.
specific_findings: The penultimate cadential chord functions as G dominant rather than F subdominant, supporting Authentic over Plagal.
The final clear harmonic arrival is C major, consistent with V–I in C.
The clip does not end on a dominant chord, so an imperfect/half-cadence reading is not supported.
The resolution is to C major rather than to a vi chord, so a broken/deceptive cadence is not supported.
The last portion is mainly tonic sustain/decay after the resolution, matching the explanation's description of the ending.
items.uncertainty: Exact inner voices and the precise labeling of the earlier D-minor preparation are partly masked by overlap and sustain, so that detail is less certain than the overall V–I cadence. No score region was supplied, so score-region relevance is not applicable.

items.heard_summary: In the supplied 14.2–21.8 s excerpt, a steady bass-and-drums/funk-like loop continues underneath a saxophone improvisation. The sax line is not a single repeated note; it moves through quick, higher-register phrases. During the later part of the clip, some sax notes sound tension-filled or chromatically inflected against the unchanging harmonic bed, then the line settles back into the groove. I do not hear a clearly sustained quotation of a familiar popular melody.
specific_findings: The rhythm-section loop remains continuous and does not audibly modulate, supporting the explanation that the background harmony stays fixed while the solo creates tension.
The saxophone plays rapid multi-note phrases rather than one repeated pitch, which contradicts choice C and supports the submitted alternative analysis.
Brief dissonant/chromatic inflections in the sax line create friction against the static backing before resolving, consistent with choice D, 'playing momentarily outside the key of the song'.
No clearly recognizable quoted melody is sustained in the excerpt, weakening choice A.
The submitted 'about 17–19 seconds' reference is broadly consistent with the audible high/fast sax activity in the clip, but exact synchronization is not credited because the timing is approximate.
items.uncertainty: Without a score or isolated harmonic reduction, 'outside the key' is an interpretive auditory judgment based on tension against the fixed loop rather than confirmed pitch names. No score region was supplied, so score-region relevance is not applicable.
